id: Resources for Immigrant Families::On the FAFSA specifically, for mixed-status families
heading: On the FAFSA specifically, for mixed-status families
text: This is one of the most common sources of fear and confusion for immigrant families, so it's worth being direct and precise about exactly what the form does and doesn't ask. The FAFSA does not ask about a parent's immigration status, at all. A parent who doesn't have a Social Security Number can still be listed as a "contributor" on the form — there is a specific, built-in way to indicate this, and it does not require inventing or borrowing a number from anyone. What determines a student's own eligibility for federal aid is the student's own status, not the parent's. A U.S. citizen or "eligible non-citizen" student (a specific government category, explained in the Financial Aid guide) can file the FAFSA and access federal aid even if a parent is undocumented. Because concerns about data privacy and immigration enforcement are real and understandably front-of-mind for many families, and because policy and practice in this specific area can shift, this is a topic where getting current, direct guidance — from a school counselor, a college's own financial aid office, or an established immigration-focused nonprofit — genuinely matters more than in most other parts of this process. Secondhand information from friends, social media, or an outdated article is a poor substitute here.

id: Resources for Immigrant Families::State aid for undocumented students, including DACA recipients
heading: State aid for undocumented students, including DACA recipients
text: Students who are themselves undocumented, including those with DACA (Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals) status, are not eligible for federal financial aid and generally should not submit a standard FAFSA. However, a meaningful number of individual states — roughly 20, plus Washington, D.C., as of recent counts, though this changes over time — offer their own state financial aid regardless of a student's federal immigration status. A few states, including Maryland and Massachusetts, have gone further and built entirely separate state aid application forms that don't require a Social Security number at all. Which states offer this, and under exactly what terms, changes over time, so it's always worth verifying your specific state's current policy directly, rather than relying on what was true even a year or two ago.

id: Resources for Immigrant Families::In-state tuition and how residency is actually decided
heading: In-state tuition and how residency is actually decided
text: At public universities, the same seat has two prices: in-state and out-of-state. The difference is frequently tens of thousands of dollars a year, which makes residency one of the largest single financial variables in this entire process — larger, often, than any scholarship a student will win. Residency is not decided by the admissions office and it is not the same question as immigration status. It is decided by the university's residency or registrar's office under rules set by the state, and those rules typically turn on things like how long the family has physically lived in the state, whether they file state taxes there, and whether the student graduated from a high school in that state. That last one matters here. A number of states have provisions allowing students who attended and graduated from a high school in the state to pay the in-state rate, on the basis of where they actually grew up. Which states, and on what exact terms, varies — and these provisions have been changed by legislatures and challenged in courts, so anything you read about them (including this) can go out of date. So the reliable move is not to trust a general article. It is to ask the specific university's residency office what documentation they require, and to ask early: many require proof covering a year or more before enrolment, which means the paperwork question arrives long before the tuition bill does. We can explain how residency classification works. We can't tell you what any particular office will decide in your situation, and you should be sceptical of any free website that claims it can. For anything status-specific, a licensed immigration attorney or an accredited non-profit legal representative is the right person — not a college website, not us, and not a notario.

id: Resources for Immigrant Families::On disclosing immigration status on college applications
heading: On disclosing immigration status on college applications
text: Many colleges do not require a student to disclose their immigration status simply to apply, and policies about whether or how status might affect an admission decision vary by school. If a family is uncertain, contacting a school's admissions office directly, or a nonprofit that specializes in exactly this question, is a safer path than guessing based on general assumptions or something read online.

id: Resources for Immigrant Families::A note on legal questions specifically
heading: A note on legal questions specifically
text: This guide, and this app more broadly, can share general information — but specific legal questions about immigration status, DACA renewal, visas, or eligibility should always go to a qualified immigration attorney or a reputable, established immigration legal nonprofit. They should never go to informal advice, or to unlicensed "notario" services — a term for unofficial, unlicensed immigration consultants — some of which are predatory and specifically target immigrant families with inaccurate or harmful advice. A school counselor or local resettlement agency can usually point a family toward a trustworthy, often free or low-cost, legal resource.

id: How to Support Your Child's Applications::What changes when your child turns 18
source_article: How to Support Your Child's Applications
heading: What changes when your child turns 18
text: There's a legal shift most families don't see coming. Under FERPA — the U.S. federal law covering education records — the rights over a student's records transfer from the parent to the student when the student turns 18 or enrols in a college, whichever happens first. The Department of Education describes the student at that point as an "eligible student." In practice this means a college may decline to discuss your child's grades, bills or records with you, even if you are paying the tuition. It is not the college being obstructive, and it isn't about you. It is the default the law sets. There are exceptions — a college is permitted to share records with parents of a student who is a dependent for tax purposes, and in health or safety emergencies — but permitted is not required, and each institution sets its own practice. Most colleges have a form a student can sign to grant a parent access. The useful thing to know is that this is a conversation to have *with your child*, before it becomes an emergency at a billing office. It's also worth naming what it reflects: from the moment they enrol, the system treats your child as the responsible adult in their own education. That is a big shift for many families, and being ready for it is easier than being surprised by it.
